claims.text: Classical molecular dynamics can be used to study the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Validated EAM or MEAM potentials are available or suitable for simulations of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will undergo more pronounced morphological evolution during heating than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will undergo more pronounced chemical evolution during heating than larger particles.
The initial particles are as-synthesized spherical FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles with diameters from 2 nm to approximately 10 nm.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a nominally random elemental distribution.
A controlled molecular-dynamics temperature ramp from room temperature to 1200 K can probe the nanoparticles' thermal response.
The simulations should represent high-vacuum or inert-atmosphere conditions.
The interatomic potentials should reproduce the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of FeCuCrCoNi.
Elemental distribution, short-range ordering, and diffusion drive local chemical segregation and structural transformations in the nanoparticles.
Increasing temperature activates atomic diffusion that can produce compositional rearrangement and phase transformation.
Increasing temperature can cause morphological restructuring of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Particle size modulates thermally activated diffusion, phase transformation, and morphological restructuring in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have greater atomic mobility than larger particles under heating.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles change less because they have lower surface-to-volume ratios.
Existing nanoscale HEA molecular-dynamics studies indicate strong correlations among particle size, diffusion, and thermally driven structural changes.
The cited studies do not directly examine FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles or systematic particle-size effects in that composition.
Prediction accuracy depends on the reliability of the interatomic potential.
Non-ideal stoichiometry and surface contamination may alter the thermal response relative to the idealized simulation.
Experimental or ab initio verification is needed to confirm the predicted size-dependent effects in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
